messages.subject: TPS grids for mean shapes not warping correctly
parts:
Hi all,

I had something pointed out to me about my mean shape TPS grids. It appears that the landmarks of the mean shapes I have plotted using plotReftoTarget for each my groups do not lie on corresponding points of their respective TPS grids

The attached file "group means 090217.jpg", shows clearly how the specimens to the left of the figure (River female and male) appear to have been plotted at different positions on their grids, relative to the specimens to the right of the figure (Reservoir female and male). A quick check scan through a few publications containing TPS grids, confirm that this is not normal.

If the landmarks of a mean shape don't lie at the same points of the grid, as the landmarks of the other mean shapes, does this mean the grids are not reflecting the complete shape transformations? If not, why could this be happening? Could it be a problem with my install of geomorph or am I doing something wrong when computing/plotting mean shapes on TPS grids?


Here's the code I used

mat <- matrix(c(1,2,3,4), 2)
layout(mat, widths=c(1,1), heights=c(1,1))# set the size of the rows and columns

ref=mshape(smeltshp.gpa$coords)

# create plot area, set margins and grid layout
mat <- matrix(c(1,2,3,4), 2)
par(mar=c(0, 0, 0, 0))
layout(mat, widths=c(1,1), heights=c(1,1))

# plot mean shapes
riv.f<-plotRefToTarget(mshape(smeltshp.gpa$coords),shpmean.riv.f, mag=5, method="TPS", links=wf)
riv.m<-plotRefToTarget(mshape(smeltshp.gpa$coords),shpmean.riv.m, mag=5, method="TPS", links=wf)
res.f<-plotRefToTarget(mshape(smeltshp.gpa$coords),shpmean.res.f, mag=5, method="TPS", links=wf)
res.m<-plotRefToTarget(mshape(smeltshp.gpa$coords),shpmean.res.m, mag=5, method="TPS", links=wf)

Everything is up to date (geomorph, R and R studio ~ December 2016) and I'm not getting any warnings or errors at any point in my analyses. I've also tried using LS.means from advanced.procD.lm to check if perhaps in the first attempt, the means were not plotted on different coord systems, only to get the same result.

Have anyone seen this before and any thoughts on why it's happening? Happy to share data for trouble shooting.

Regards,


Daniel.

parts:
Dear Daniel,

The reason (I think) that you are not getting the results you expect is because you are magnifying your deformation.  What this accomplishes, essentially, is to take the vector between any reference point and the target point, and rather than stop at the target, continue on along the vector to emphasize the shape change.  Collectively, over all landmarks, a deformation grid highlights the areas where there is more change along these vectors.  (One could also just plot the vectors, themselves.  A mag = 5 should increase the length of the vectors about 5x.)

Here is an example using our first example from the help file to illustrate that (1) yes, the target points do fall where they should on the grids, unless (2) the magnification is changed, in which the grid points project beyond what would be expected from the target, based on the relationship between the reference and target.  

Hopefully this is clear.  If not, I probably misunderstood your concern.

Mike

data(plethodon) 
Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethodon$land)    #GPA-alignment
ref<-mshape(Y.gpa$coords)
plotRefToTarget(ref,Y.gpa$coords[,,39])
points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex = 0.5)
points(Y.gpa$coords[,,39], pch=19, col="red", cex = 0.5)

plotRefToTarget(ref,Y.gpa$coords[,,39], mag = 5)
points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex = 0.5)
points(Y.gpa$coords[,,39], pch=19, col="red", cex = 0.5)

Hi Mike,

That explains it, though I don't see why this might have been written into geomorph this way, for one main reason; while it obviously isn't a problem where the shape transformations between groups are so large that magnification is unnecessary (i.e. inter-specific comparisons), but in the case of subtle intra-specific changes, where a magnification of 3x-5x might be required, a critical reviewer might be inclined to question whether or not these shape transformations were plotted correctly for the reasons I outlined earlier, thus potentially putting otherwise quality research onto thin ice.

Could something like this be achieved manually in geomorph or otherwise? 

As you say, the magnified vectors can be plotted instead, but they don't quite capture the shape transformations as well as the grids and the grids appear to be the most commonly used, and recognized way of doing it.

Any thoughts or suggestions would be appreciated.

Regards,

Daniel.

Daniel,

I don’t understand your concern.  I don’t think we are doing anything special in geomorph that is done differently in tpsRegr.  I chased down one of the references I think you meant (Franssen 2011).  It is clear in his figure 4 that at 1x and 3x, the target landmarks are not in the same place.  He also chose to use both grids and vectors in different plots.  In the vector plots, rather than use the consensus configuration, he used one mean to map onto the other.  These are all consistent with plotRefToTarget options.

I’ll emphasize this again in a different way.  When using a magnification and the consensus configuration (overall mean) as the reference, the following is happening.  The transformation grid shows how shape changes as one moves from the origin (of the projection into tangent space, probably) in a direction toward the target shape.  At the target, one can visualize the shape change, but as you said, this might be subtle.  Using a magnification means continuing on this path, farther from the origin and past the target.  One is hypothesizing what the shape change would look like beyond the target, but to do that, a configuration that is NOT the target becomes the target.  There is simply no mathematical justification for increased deformation without a change in target points.  This does not make sense, and I would be shocked if tpsRegr does that.  (Maybe somebody who uses both tpsRegr and geomorph can verify.  I have not used tpsRegr for years and have a Mac, so I cannot verify this.)

One could hypothetically generate a grid with magnification and superimpose points for the target (like I did in the last example), without including points for the hypothetical target, which seems to achieve what you propose.  However, to me this is a mistake, especially if the magnification is much larger than 1x.  Alternatively, one could change the grid density.  Sometimes using more little squares rather than few large ones visually emphasizes the deformation more at 1x.  

Anyway, either I am missing your point or a critical reviewer who would be inclined to question if the shape transformations were plotted correctly, expecting the points of the target to match up with the target of the magnified shape change, would be incorrect in their expectation.  

I did not receive an attachment, so I might be missing what your were intending.

Mike

Mike

Dear Daniel,

 

The reason (I think) that you are not getting the results you expect is because you are magnifying your deformation.  What this accomplishes, essentially, is to take the vector between any reference point and the target point, and rather than stop at the target, continue on along the vector to emphasize the shape change.  Collectively, over all landmarks, a deformation grid highlights the areas where there is more change along these vectors.  (One could also just plot the vectors, themselves.  A mag = 5 should increase the length of the vectors about 5x.)

 

Here is an example using our first example from the help file to illustrate that (1) yes, the target points do fall where they should on the grids, unless (2) the magnification is changed, in which the grid points project beyond what would be expected from the target, based on the relationship between the reference and target.  

 

Hopefully this is clear.  If not, I probably misunderstood your concern.

 

Mike

 

data(plethodon) 

Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethodon$land)    #GPA-alignment

ref<-mshape(Y.gpa$coords)

plotRefToTarget(ref,Y.gpa$coords[,,39])

points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex = 0.5)

points(Y.gpa$coords[,,39], pch=19, col="red", cex = 0.5)

 

plotRefToTarget(ref,Y.gpa$coords[,,39], mag = 5)

points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex = 0.5)

points(Y.gpa$coords[,,39], pch=19, col="red", cex = 0.5)
